column2: Then, seeing nothing to eat on the road, the ungrateful man, tiger among men, thought this in his mind.
This lord of cranes is at my side, a heap of meat; killing him and taking him, I shall go off quickly.
The king of cranes, trusting, slept at his side then; but the ungrateful, evil-souled man, wishing to kill him, stayed awake.
Then with a blazing brand he struck down the trusting one; and having killed him he was joyful and did not see the consequence.
Having singed off his feathers he cooked him in the fire; taking him and the gold, the brahmana went off very quickly.
Then, the next day, Virupaksha said to his son, "I do not see Rajadharma, the best of birds, today, my son.
He always goes to worship Brahma at the early twilight, and he never goes home without seeing me.
Two nights and both twilights he has not come to my house; so my heart is not at ease; let that friend be sought.
That lowest of the twice-born, devoid of study and lacking Vedic lustre, went to him; I fear he may have killed him.
By his signs I marked him as ill-conducted, evil-minded, without rites, dreadful in form, black, like a low robber."
The king wept on seeing him, with his ministers and priest, and there was a great cry of anguish in his house.
With women and children the city was uneasy at heart; then the king said to his son, "Let this sinner be slain.
With his flesh let all these feast as they wish: sinful in conduct, sinful in deed, sinful in soul, sinful in resolve; it is my judgment that he should be killed by you, rakshasas."
Thus told by the lord of the rakshasas, the rakshasas of dreadful valour did not wish to eat him, saying, "He is a doer of sin."
Let this lowest of men be given to the robbers, good sir, today, the night-roamers said to the lord of the rakshasas, great king.
Bowing their heads to the ground, they said to the lord of the rakshasa hosts, "You should not give us him to eat; his sin."
So be it, the lord of the rakshasas said to the night-roamers; "let this ungrateful man be given to the robbers today, rakshasas."
Thus told, his servants, spears and clubs in hand, cut that sinner into pieces and gave him to the robbers.
And the robbers too did not wish to eat that doer of sin; even flesh-eaters, king of kings, do not eat the ungrateful.
For the killer of a brahmana, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and one who has broken his vow, atonement is prescribed, king; for the ungrateful there is none.
The betrayer of friends, the cruel, the ungrateful, the lowest of men, such as these are not eaten even by flesh-eaters, worms and others.
There, king, the lord of the rakshasas kindled a fire and heated the king of cranes, and performed the rites for the dead according to rule.
At that time the goddess Surabhi, the auspicious daughter of Daksha, appeared above him, giving milk.
From her mouth a froth mixed with milk fell, sinless one, and it fell on the pyre of Rajadharma.
Thereby the king of cranes was revived, sinless one; rising up, he met Virupaksha.
Then the king of the gods came to Virupaksha's city and said to Virupaksha, "By good fortune he lives."
And Indra told Virupaksha the old story of how the curse had once been given by Brahma to Rajadharma.

When the lord of cranes did not go to worship Brahma, then in anger the Grandfather said this to the crane-lord:
mahabharata:12:167.9	'Because that fool, the lowest of cranes, did not come to my assembly, that evil-souled one will soon meet death.'
mahabharata:12:167.10	By his word he was killed by Gautama, and by that same nectar sprinkled, the crane was revived.
Then Rajadharma, bowing to Purandara, said, "If you have shown me favour, Purandara, let my dear friend Gautama be revived."
Understanding his words, Vasava, bull among men, revived Gautama and gave him back to his friend.
The lord of cranes, king, having found him with his goods and baggage, embraced his friend with the highest affection.
Then Rajadharma, lord of cranes, sent off that doer of sin with his wealth, and entered his own dwelling.
The crane went as was fitting to the assembly of Brahma, and Brahma honoured that great soul with hospitality.
And Gautama, reaching that Shabara dwelling again, begot sons by the shudra woman, doers of evil.
A great curse was laid on him then by the hosts of gods: "Having long begotten sons on the womb of a remarried widow, he will go to a great hell; this one is ungrateful, lord."
All this Narada told me long ago, Bharata; recalling that great tale, bull among men, I too have related it all to you as it was.
Where is fame for the ungrateful, where position, where happiness? The ungrateful is not to be trusted; for the ungrateful there is no atonement.
Treachery to a friend should not be done by a man, especially; the betrayer of a friend goes to a dreadful, endless hell.
One should always be grateful, and desire friends, sinless one; from a friend truth arises, from a friend strength arises; the wise should honour a friend with the best hospitality.
The sinful, ungrateful, shameless, the betrayer of friends, the ember of the family, the doer of sin, the lowest of men, should be abandoned by the wise.
This sinner has been described to you by me, best of those who uphold dharma, the betrayer of friends and ungrateful; what more do you wish to hear?"
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing these words spoken by the great-souled Bhishma, Yudhishthira became glad at heart, Janamejaya.
[Bhishma said:] "Dharma is ordained everywhere, leading to heaven; austerity has truth as its fruit; for dharma of many doors, no act here is fruitless.
In whatever discipline a man reaches certainty, he knows that alone and no other, best of the Bharatas.
As the machinery of the world turns, empty of substance, so detachment arises here; there is no doubt.
Thus, with the world resolved in this way and full of faults, Yudhishthira, the wise man should strive for the sake of his own liberation."
[Yudhishthira said:] "When wealth is lost, or wife, son or father dead, by what wisdom should one drive away grief? Tell me that, grandsire."
[Bhishma said:] "When wealth is lost, or wife, son or father dead, thinking 'Alas, the sorrow,' one should practise the remedy of grief.
Here too they cite this ancient tale, how a certain brahmana spoke words to Senajit.
Seeing the king afflicted with grief for his son, overcome with sorrow, his face downcast, the brahmana spoke."
[Senajit said:] "What wisdom, what austerity, brahmana, what concentration, rich in austerity, what knowledge or learning is yours, by which you are not despondent?"
[The brahmana said:] "See beings everywhere bound in sorrow; even this self is not mine, nor is all the earth mine.
As it is with me, so with others: by this thought I have no pain; having gained this wisdom, I neither rejoice nor grieve.
As a log and a log meet in the great ocean and, meeting, part, so is the meeting of beings.
So sons and grandsons, kinsmen and relatives: no attachment should be made to them, for separation from them is certain.
He came from unseen and has gone again to the unseen; he does not know you nor you him; who are you, and for whom do you grieve?
Sorrow is born of the pain of craving, and pleasure of the pain of sorrow; from pleasure sorrow is born, and so again and again; after pleasure comes sorrow, after sorrow pleasure.
Having fallen from pleasure into sorrow, you will fall again into pleasure; one does not always get sorrow, nor always pleasure.
Friends are not enough for happiness, enemies not enough for sorrow; wisdom is not enough for wealth, nor wealth for happiness.
Neither intelligence leads to gain of wealth nor stupidity to poverty; the wise one knows the turning course of the world, not another.
The wise and the foolish, the brave and the timid, the dull and the poet, the weak and the strong, happiness serves the one who has his share.
The cow gives milk to the calf, the herdsman, the owner and the thief; whoever drinks her milk, it is settled she is his.
Those who are most foolish in the world and those who have gone beyond intellect: these men prosper in happiness; the man in between suffers.
The wise delight in the extremes, they do not delight in the middle; they call reaching the end happiness, and the middle between the ends sorrow.
Those who have attained the happiness of the intellect, beyond the pairs, without envy: neither gains nor losses ever trouble them.
But those who have not attained intellect and have passed beyond foolishness rejoice excessively and come to torment.
The fools are ever joyful, like hosts of gods in heaven, but puffed up with great pride, they are senseless.
Happiness has sorrow as its end in sloth; sorrow has happiness as its rise in skill; prosperity with fortune dwells in the skilled, not the idle.
Whether pleasure or pain, hateful or dear, whatever comes, one should take as it comes, with a heart unconquered.
Thousands of causes of grief and hundreds of causes of joy enter the fool day by day, not the wise man.
Grief does not touch the man who is intelligent, of trained wisdom, attentive and free of envy, self-controlled and master of his senses.
Resorting to this wisdom, the wise man should live with guarded mind; grief does not deserve to touch one who knows rise and setting.
That by reason of which there would be grief, fear or pain, or from which exertion arises, even one part of that should be given up.
Whatever one gives up of desires, that fills up his happiness; the man who follows desires perishes along with his desires.
The pleasure of desire in the world and the great divine pleasure do not equal a sixteenth part of the pleasure of the end of craving.
The deed done in a former body, good or bad, serves the wise, the foolish and the brave according to what was done.
So indeed these pleasants and unpleasants, sorrows and joys, turn about among living beings.

So, resorting to this wisdom, one should live happily, endowed with virtue; one should hold all desires in disgust and put attachments behind him; this is the load in the heart; this is death, made of mind.
When one draws in desires from all sides as a tortoise its limbs, then the self-light and the self grow serene in the self alone.
When anything is conceived with the sense of mine, all of it then becomes a cause of torment.
When one does not fear and others do not fear one, when he neither wishes nor hates, then he attains Brahman.
Having abandoned both truth and untruth, grief and joy, fear and fearlessness, the dear and the undear, you will be of tranquil soul.
When the wise man does no wrong to any being in deed, mind or speech, then he attains Brahman.
That craving, hard for the ill-minded to give up, which does not age as one ages, the disease that ends in death: happiness is for one who gives up that craving.
Here verses sung by Pingala are heard, king, how even in hard times she found eternal dharma.
The courtesan Pingala, bereft of her lover at the tryst, then, in distress, took up a calm mind.
[Pingala said:] "Mad, I lived long with a lover who was not mad; though he was near and delighting me, I did not know him before.
A house with a single pillar and nine doors: I shall shut it; for what woman, seeing a lover come in here, would think 'this is my lover'?
Those without love in the form of love, rogues in the shape of hell, shall not deceive me again; I am awake, I am watchful.
Even a loss becomes gain by fate or by past deeds; I have awakened, without form of hope; today I am not without mastery of my senses.
The hopeless sleeps happily; hopelessness is the highest happiness; having made hope hopeless, Pingala sleeps happily."
[Bhishma said:] "By these and other reasoned words of the brahmana, King Senajit was set right and rejoiced happily."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of a father with his son; learn it, Yudhishthira.
A certain twice-born, Partha, devoted to study, had a wise son, named Medhavin.
The son, skilled in the dharma of liberation and in wealth, discerning the truth of the world, said to his father, who was devoted to study:
Father, what should a wise man do, knowing that the life of men quickly slips away? Tell me, father, in proper order and as it truly is, by which I may practise dharma.

[The father said:] "Having studied the Vedas in celibacy, son, one should wish for sons for the purification of the ancestors; having set up the fires according to rule, performed sacrifices and rites, one should enter the forest and desire to be a sage."
[The son said:] "With the world struck down in this way and surrounded on all sides, with unfailing ones falling, why do you speak as if you were wise?"
[The father said:] "How is the world struck down, or by what surrounded? Which unfailing ones fall here? Why do you seem to frighten me?"
[The son said:] "The world is struck down by death and surrounded by old age; these days and nights fall; why do you not wake?
While desires are unattained, death comes to a man, gathering him like one picking ears of grain, his mind elsewhere; like a she-wolf with a lamb, death carries him off.
Do today what is best; let this time not pass you; while tasks remain undone, death drags one away.
Tomorrow's work should be done today, the afternoon's in the forenoon; death does not wait whether it is done or not; who knows for whom the army of death will camp today?
One should be devoted to dharma in youth itself, for life has no cause; when dharma is done, there is fame here and happiness hereafter.
Overcome by delusion, bent on sons and wives, doing what should and should not be done, one gives them nourishment.
The man intoxicated with sons and cattle, with mind attached, death carries off, like a great flood a sleeping tiger.
The man gathering, unsated in desires, death carries off, as a tiger a beast.
This is done, this is to be done, this is half done: the End brings under his sway one so striving and attached to pleasure.
One who has not got the fruit of his works, attached to the fruit, attached to field, shop and house, death carries off.
When death, old age, disease and sorrow of many causes cling to the body, how can you stay as if at ease?
The End follows the embodied one at birth for his end, and old age follows; these states cling to the moving and unmoving by both.
That delight of one dwelling in a village is a house of death; the forest is the cattle-pen of the gods, so scripture says.
That delight of one dwelling in a village is a binding rope; the virtuous go, cutting it; the wicked do not cut it.
He who does not harm others' lives by mind, speech or body, or by deeds that take away life, is not bound.
No one at all can hold back the army of death as it comes, except by truth that is not to be abandoned; in truth, nectar is lodged.
Therefore, one whose conduct is the vow of truth, devoted to the discipline of truth, delighting in truth, equal and self-controlled, should conquer the End by truth alone.
Nectar and death, both are established in the body; through delusion one reaches death; through truth one reaches nectar.
So I, non-violent, seeking truth, outside desire and anger, equal in pleasure and pain, secure, shall leave death behind, like one immortal.
Delighting in the sacrifice of peace, self-controlled, a sage established in the sacrifice of Brahman, I shall be a sacrifice of speech, mind and action in the northern course.
How can one like me, wise, sacrifice with violent animal sacrifices, perishable, or with kshatriya sacrifices, like a goblin?
He whose speech and mind are always rightly set, whose austerity, renunciation and yoga are such, gains everything.
There is no eye like knowledge, no strength like knowledge, no sorrow like attachment, no happiness like renunciation.
Born in the self by the self, established in the self, even without offspring, I shall be in the self alone; offspring do not carry me across.
For a brahmana there is no wealth like this: oneness, equanimity, truthfulness, steadiness in conduct, freedom from the pairs, honesty, and withdrawal from actions.
What are wealth and kinsmen to you, what wives, brahmana, since you will die? Seek the self that has entered the cave; where has your grandfather gone, and your father?"
[Bhishma said:] "Hearing this speech of his son, the father did so, king; so you too should act, devoted to truth and dharma."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, sung by Shamyaka when freed, who had reached peace.
A certain brahmana, who had taken up renunciation, once said to me, afflicted by a bad wife, bad clothes and hunger:
'Born in this world, from birth onward a man meets sorrows and joys of many kinds.
If either of the two leads him on his way, he should not rejoice on gaining pleasure, nor burn on gaining sorrow.
You do not do what is best for yourself, nor what you strive for; even without desire, always lift the yoke.
Having nothing, wandering, you will taste happiness; one with nothing sleeps happily and rises happily.
Having nothing is happiness in the world, wholesome, auspicious, free of disease, without enemies; this is hard to get yet easy for the good.
Of one with nothing, pure, endowed in every way, looking at the three worlds, I see nothing equal.
Him, ever moving as he wishes, sleeping without a bed, with his arm as pillow, at peace, the dwellers in heaven praise.
The rich man, possessed by anger and greed, senseless, squinting, dry-mouthed, sinful, with a frowning face,
biting his lower lip, angry, speaking harshly: who would wish to look at him, if he were willing to give the earth?
Constant dwelling with fortune bewilders the unwise; she steals his mind as the wind a cloud of autumn.
Then pride of beauty and pride of wealth take hold of him: "I am well-born, I am accomplished, I am not a mere man"; by these three causes his mind is drenched.
With his mind drenched, he casts off the enjoyments saved by his fathers, and, reduced, thinks taking others' property good.
Him, who has transgressed the limit and takes from here and there, kings restrain, like greedy hunters a deer with arrows.
Thus these sorrows of many kinds, born of touch of the body, come to a man here.
One should practise the remedy for these great sorrows by intelligence, knowing the dharma of the world, the unsteady with the steady.
Without giving up one does not gain happiness, without giving up one does not find the highest, without giving up one does not sleep without fear; giving up all, be happy.'
This was described to me at Hastinapura by the brahmana Shamyaka long ago; therefore I hold renunciation to be supreme."
[Bhishma said:] "Equality toward all, freedom from exertion, truthful speech, detachment, and freedom from contentiousness: the man who has these is happy.
The elders say these five steps are for peace; this is heaven, dharma, and the highest happiness of the good.
Here too they cite this ancient tale, sung by Manki out of detachment; learn it, Yudhishthira.
Manki, striving for wealth and repeatedly frustrated, with some remaining wealth bought a pair of young bullocks.
The two well-yoked bullocks, going out to be broken in, suddenly ran at a camel sitting between them.
When the two reached him, the camel, enraged, stood up, lifted the two onto his shoulder, and ran off at great speed.
Seeing the two bullocks carried off by that tormenting camel, and dying, Manki said this there.
'Wealth cannot be sought even by the skilled unless it is ordained, even joined with faith and rightly following effort.
Two ornaments hang from the camel's neck; my two dear calves are carried off; this is surely pure fate; there is no human effort.
Even if human effort is found at any time, when sought, that too stands as fate alone.
Therefore detachment alone is to be reached here by one who wants happiness; the despondent sleeps happily, hopeless in the pursuit of wealth.
Ah, well said by Shuka, free of everything, setting out for the great forest from Janaka's house.
One who could obtain all desires and one who gives them all up: the giving up of all desires surpasses their attainment.
No one has ever gone to the end of all longings; in body and life the craving of the dull grows.
Turn back from longings, be calm, be disgusted, my friend; you have been deceived again and again, and you are still not disgusted, body.
If I am not to be destroyed by you, if you so delight in me, do not engage me in greed in vain, you who love wealth.
The wealth you have heaped up has been lost again and again; when will you let go, fool, wealth-seeker, lover of wealth?
Ah, my folly, that I am bought by you; would a man ever become the servant of others?
Neither those before nor after have reached the end of desires; giving up all undertakings, I am awake, I am watchful.
Surely your heart, desire, is made of the firm essence of the thunderbolt, since though seized by hundreds of evils it does not split in a hundred.
I give up you, desire, and whatever is dear to you; seeking happiness for myself, I find happiness in the self.
Desire, I know your root; you are born from conception; I shall not conceive you, and you will not be with your root.
The seeking of wealth is not happy; after gaining it, worry increases; loss of the gained is like death; whether it is gained or not.
Who gets nothing after death? What is more painful? One is not satisfied with what is got and seeks more.
Wealth, ever craving, is sweet like Ganga water; it dissolves intoxication; I am awake; let it go.
Let the host of beings that has resorted to this body of mine go from here as it likes, or stay as it pleases.
I have no affection for you here, who follow desire and greed; leaving all of you, I take refuge in truth alone.
Seeing all beings in the body and in my own mind, fixing intellect in yoga, learning, goodness, and mind in Brahman,
I shall roam unattached, happy, free of disease in the worlds, so that you will not again put me into sorrows as you have.
Driven out by you I have no other refuge; for craving, grief and fatigue you, desire, are always the source.
I think loss of wealth the greater sorrow, the greatest of all; relatives despise and friends despise one who has fallen from wealth.
With thousands of humiliations come faults in poverty and wealth; and the little portion of pleasure is made of pains.
Robbers formerly strike a man, saying "he has wealth"; people are troubled by various conflicts and ever alarmed.
I have long known that dull greed is sorrow; whatever you cling to, desire, you follow that.
You do not know the truth; you are a child, hard to satisfy, never full, like fire; you know neither the easy nor the hard.
Hard to fill like the nether world, you wish to bind me with sorrows; today I cannot be engaged again by you, desire.
Having reached detachment through loss of wealth by chance, and gained the highest peace, I no longer think of desires.
I bear excessive hardships here; unwise, I do not wake; deceived by loss of wealth, I lie with fever in all my limbs.
I give you up, desire, leaving all movements of the mind; you will not again delight in me as in a woven cloth.
I shall forgive those who do not forgive, I shall not harm though harmed, freed from hate I shall speak kindly, disregarding the unkind.
Satisfied, with senses at ease, ever living on what comes, I shall not make you, my enemy, fulfilled.
Know that I have come to detachment, ease, satisfaction, peace, truth, self-control, forbearance and compassion for all beings as my refuge.
Therefore let desire, greed, craving and meanness leave me as I stand firm; I am now abiding in goodness.
Having abandoned desire, greed, anger and harshness, today I am not under the sway of greed; I shall not meet sorrow, being master of myself.
Whatever one gives up of desires, that fills up his happiness; one ever under the power of desire meets only sorrow.
When a man shakes off desires, whatever dust there is, sorrow born of desire and anger, shamelessness and discontent, goes.
I have entered Brahman like a pool in summer entered for cold; I am calm, I am cool, I sit in pure happiness.
The pleasure of desire in the world and the great divine pleasure do not equal a sixteenth part of the pleasure of the end of craving.
Having killed desire, the best enemy, with myself as the seventh, and reached the unslayable city of Brahman, I shall be happy like a king.'
Resorting to this wisdom, Manki reached detachment; giving up all desires, he gained the great happiness of Brahman.
By the loss of his bullocks, Manki is said to have reached immortality; he cut the root of desire and by that gained great happiness.
Here too they cite this ancient tale, sung by Janaka, king of Videha, when he had found peace.
'Infinite, alas, is my wealth, for I have nothing at all; when Mithila is on fire, nothing of mine is burnt.'"
His tenth son, Bharata, named Dasha ashva, was king at Mahishmati, righteous-souled, of true valour.
And near that very place was his sacrificial ground; there the righteous-souled lord of the earth, Marutta, sacrificed duly, with all the protectors of the subjects, that ruler of men.
And you too, dear, share the fruit of austerity, for you are a king; kings share the fruit of good, or of the other.
Then that dreadful club of iron, like a thunderbolt, appeared; with it Krishna killed those who were before him.
[Dharma said:] "Abandoning Bhima and Arjuna, both your brothers, you wished for Nakula to live, wanting equality between the two mothers.
Then a wind blew, pleasant to touch, bearing holy fragrance, auspicious, cool, coming from the presence of the gods, exceedingly so, Bharata.
